title: Who I am
job: Introduce yourself and state what you like
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The neutral word order is the English one — subject, verb, object — so Я люблю чай comes out in the order you already think in. Russian can move the pieces around for emphasis, and M10 shows what that does; nothing in this module needs it.

There is no present-tense "to be". Я студент is the whole sentence — two words, "I student" — and nothing has been left out. Reaching for a word to fill the gap gives Я есть студент, which is the single most English mistake you can make in Russian. Only the PRESENT is empty: the past (был) and the future (буду) are real words, and they arrive in M5 and M6.

There are no articles at all. книга is "book", "a book" and "the book"; nothing on the page tells them apart. That is a whole system with nothing to learn — but the work English gives a and the has to go somewhere, and in Russian it goes into word order: M10 is where that is paid.

A name is given with Меня зовут — literally "me they-call". It is a fixed phrase, not a sentence you assemble: Меня зовут Иван is "my name is Ivan", and Моё имя — Иван, though grammatical, is not how anyone introduces themselves.

из ("from") changes the ending of the place after it: Индия → Индии, Москва → Москвы. Russian has six such endings — cases — and this is the first one you meet. Do not try to work it out here: learn Я из … with the shape it takes, and M3 starts teaching the endings properly.

Every noun has a gender, and its ending is the first clue: a consonant at the end means masculine (чай, хлеб, язык), -а or -я means feminine (книга, Москва, Индия), -о or -е means neuter (молоко). The clue is not a law — nouns ending in -ь can be either and must be learned with their gender, and кофе is masculine in spite of its -е. Learn a noun and its gender together.

The thing you like follows the verb, in the object case: Я люблю чай. In this module the object never actually changes shape, because masculine things that are not alive (чай, язык) and neuter things (молоко) look identical in the object case. M3 is where the ending finally moves — and it moves on feminine nouns.

In writing, when both halves of an "X is Y" sentence are nouns, a dash stands where English puts is: Анна — студентка. After a pronoun it is left out: Я студентка. The dash is punctuation, not a word — it is never said out loud.

words.note: Two words that work as one: зовут is "they call" and меня is "me", so the phrase is "they call me …" with nobody in particular doing the calling. This, and not Моё имя, is how a Russian gives a name. Learn it whole — the pieces are not worth separating until much later.
A man's name, carried over unchanged — swap in your own. Russian writes names with a capital letter, exactly as English does.

sentences.trap: Меня зовут is Иван looks like it is missing a verb, so English speakers want to add one: Меня зовут есть Иван. There is nothing to add — зовут is already the verb of the sentence.
sentences.sound: me-NYA za-VOOT. Both unstressed о sounds come out as a short "a" — this is the single most useful pronunciation fact in Russian, and it applies to every word on this rung.

variations.changed: swap the name — Меня зовут itself never moves
меня → вас: the same verb, now asking somebody else. M2 takes this apart
меня → её: the phrase names a third person without changing зовут

mistake.why: Grammatical, and nobody says it — it reads the way "My appellation is Ivan" reads in English. Меня зовут Иван is the sentence.

sentences.usage: The first line of any introduction, in any register.
sentences.mnemonic: зовут is "they call". Your name is what they call you — меня зовут.

words.note: "Very", and it sits in front of whatever it strengthens, exactly as in English.
"Pleasant", in the shape Russian uses when there is no particular thing being described — it is the whole reply on its own. M9 builds a family of these: мне холодно, "to me [it is] cold".

sentences.trap: There is no "it", no "is" and no "to meet you" anywhere in it. English needs four words of scaffolding for a formula Russian says in two.
sentences.sound: O-chen pree-YAT-na. The final -о of приятно is unstressed, so it comes out as "a"; the ь on очень only softens the н, and is never a sound of its own.

variations.changed: a name after a comma — the standard way to close the formula
drop очень: shorter and cooler, the same reply with less warmth in it
swap what очень strengthens — the frame takes any of these words. M2 teaches хорошо

mistake.why: The Это is English scaffolding creeping in. The formula is two words and stands alone.

sentences.usage: Said on being introduced, immediately after hearing a name. Both people say it.
sentences.mnemonic: Not "nice to meet you" but "very pleasant" — the reaction, with the sentence around it left out.

words.note: One pronoun in three shapes, and Russian picks the shape by the job: я does the acting (Я студент), меня is the one acted on (Меня зовут — "they call ME"), and мне is the one something is done TO or FOR (M9's мне холодно, "to me [it is] cold"). English does the same trick with I / me, just less often.
A male student. A woman is студентка — a different word, not a different ending on this one, and it has its own row on S07. Masculine, because it ends in a consonant.

sentences.trap: English cannot say this sentence: it needs am and it needs a. Russian has neither, and adding either one is wrong — Я есть студент and Я один студент are both mistakes, not politer versions.
sentences.sound: ya stoo-DYENT. The е after д softens it, so it is "dyent", not "dent" — that softening is what most of Russian's е letters are doing.

variations.cue: I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: студент → студентка: the sentence changes with who is speaking, which English never does here
я → a name: still no verb anywhere in the sentence
не in front of the missing verb — where nothing is, не goes before the word it denies. M3 teaches this properly

mistake.why: есть is a real Russian word, but not this one: the present tense of "to be" simply is not written. Я студент is the whole sentence.

sentences.usage: Saying what you do — work or study — when you meet someone.
sentences.mnemonic: Two words, two ideas: who, and what. Russian charges you nothing for the "is".

words.note: "From", in the sense of coming out of somewhere. It always changes the ending of the place that follows it — that is not optional and not a style, it is what Russian prepositions do.

India. Индия is the dictionary shape; Индии is what из takes (Я из Индии) and also what в takes (в Индии, "in India") — one written shape doing two jobs, which is normal in Russian and worth expecting.

sentences.trap: Я из Индия copies the dictionary form straight into the sentence, the way English would. из never leaves a place unchanged.
sentences.sound: ya eez EEN-dee-ee. из loses its "z" sound to a "s" before some consonants, but before a vowel — as here — it stays a clean z.

variations.changed: swap the place — Россия shifts to России exactly as Индия shifted
я → a name: the place keeps its из-shape whoever is speaking
a question with nothing moved — only the mark and the voice change. M2's lesson

mistake.why: из takes a changed ending, always: Я из Индии. The dictionary form Индия is for the subject of a sentence, not for after a preposition.

sentences.usage: Where you are from — the second or third line of any introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: из pulls something OUT of a place, and pulling it out bends the ending.

words.note: Moscow. Москва is the dictionary shape and the subject shape; Москвы is what из takes. A third shape, Москве, arrives in M7 for "in Moscow" — all three are the same word, and they all live here.

sentences.trap: The two из sentences take different endings — Индии but Москвы — and there is no way to guess which from English. The ending depends on how the word itself ends, and this level teaches the pairs rather than the system.
sentences.sound: ya eez mask-VY. The stress is on the last syllable and the first о is unstressed, so nobody says "MOSS-cow"; ы is a hard, back "i" made with the tongue pulled away from the teeth.

variations.changed: я → a name, and still no verb in the sentence
back to the dictionary shape — with no preposition in front of it, Москва does not bend
the same words as a question: nothing moves, only the mark

mistake.why: из bends the place after it. Я из Москвы — and the -ы here is a different ending from Индии's -и, because the two words end differently.

sentences.usage: Naming a city rather than a country — the same frame, and it is the more common answer.
sentences.mnemonic: Москва has an а on the end; из swaps that а for ы.

words.note: The pointing word, and it does the whole job on its own: Это Анна is "this is Anna" with no verb anywhere. It never changes shape when it opens a sentence like this, whatever it points at — Это книга, Это Москва, Это молоко.
A woman's name. Both н letters are written and both are said — a held "nn", not the single n of English "Anna".

sentences.trap: English needs is here and cannot drop it. Russian supplies Это and stops — putting anything between Это and the name is the mistake.
sentences.sound: E-ta AN-na. The final о of Это is unstressed, so it is "E-ta"; the double н of Анна is genuinely held, roughly "AN-na".

variations.changed: swap who is being introduced — Это never moves
point at a role instead of a person — and there is still no word for "a"
the same two words asked instead of told — Russian moves nothing to make a question

mistake.why: The same reflex as Я есть студент, one sentence later. Это Анна is complete.

sentences.usage: Introducing somebody else, or pointing at a thing and naming it.
sentences.mnemonic: Это points, and pointing is enough — Russian does not also need to say that the thing is.

words.note: A female student — its own word, built from студент with -ка, and feminine because it ends in -а. Russian names most jobs twice like this, and which one you write depends on who is being described, not on who is speaking.

sentences.trap: The dash is not a translation of is. It is a punctuation mark that marks the gap where English would put a verb, and it appears only when both halves are nouns — never after я or вы.
sentences.sound: AN-na stoo-DYENT-ka. Nothing is said where the dash is: it is a pause at most.

variations.changed: the same frame about a man — студентка → студент

variations.cue: I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: a pronoun subject, so the dash goes: it is written only between two nouns

variations.cue: Anna is a student from Moscow
variations.changed: the из phrase hangs off the second noun, exactly as in English

mistake.why: The dash belongs between two nouns. With a pronoun in front, Russian writes Я студентка and nothing else.

sentences.usage: Saying what somebody else does — the third line of an introduction, after their name.
sentences.mnemonic: Two nouns need something between them, so Russian draws a line where English says is.

words.note: One verb for both "like" and "love", and about food or music it is simply "like". The ending names who: люблю is I, любит is he or she, любите is you (the polite вы this course speaks). The б in люблю appears only in the I-form — a quirk of this verb, not a rule; M4 sorts out endings properly.
Tea. Masculine, because it ends in a consonant sound — and because it is a thing rather than a living creature, it looks exactly the same as the object of a sentence as it does in the dictionary.

sentences.trap: люблю is not too strong. English keeps love for people and big feelings, so "I love tea" sounds odd; Russian uses люблю for anything you are fond of, and saying it about tea is completely ordinary.
sentences.sound: ya lyoo-BLYOO chai. The л is soft in both syllables — the tongue is up against the roof of the mouth, closer to English "million" than to "loop".

variations.changed: люблю → любит: the ending swaps the person, and no other word moves
люблю → любите for the person you are speaking to, and the sentence becomes a question with nothing added
a describing word slots in front of the noun, exactly where English puts it

mistake.why: чай does not change here. Bending the ending is what M3's feminine nouns do; a masculine thing like чай stays as it is.

sentences.usage: Likes of every kind — food, drink, music, a language.
sentences.mnemonic: люблю covers everything from tea to people; Russian simply does not have a weaker word for it.

words.note: Milk. Neuter, because it ends in -о — and neuter things, like masculine things that are not alive, look identical whether they are the subject of a sentence or its object. So молоко does not move here.

sentences.trap: There is no "the" and no "some" in front of it. Я люблю молоко covers "I like milk" in general, which is the only reading this sentence has.
sentences.sound: ma-la-KO. Three о letters, and only the stressed one is really an "o" — the other two flatten to "a". Russian written with its stress on the page would help here, and Russian is never written that way.

variations.changed: люблю → любит: the person changes and молоко does not
the polite you-form, asked rather than told
the same word as the subject of a pointing sentence — proof that it never bends

mistake.why: A neuter noun does not change in the object slot. Я люблю молоко — молока is a different shape with a different job, and this sentence has no use for it.

sentences.usage: Everyday likes and dislikes about food and drink.
sentences.mnemonic: Neuter nouns are the lazy ones: subject or object, they never get up.

words.note: "Russian" as a description, and it goes in front of what it describes, exactly as in English. Russian writes nationalities and languages with a small letter — русский, never Русский — which is the opposite of the English habit.
Language — and also the tongue in your mouth, the same double meaning English once had. Masculine, ends in a consonant, and does not change in the object slot.

sentences.trap: The language is русский язык, two words, and dropping the noun does not work the way "I like Russian" does in English. Русский on its own describes a Russian man.
sentences.sound: ROO-skee ya-ZYK. The double с in русский is one long "ss", and the ы of язык is that hard back "i" again, stressed this time.

variations.changed: люблю → любит, and the two-word object travels together

variations.cue: Do you like the Russian language?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, as a question
swap the noun and русский comes along unchanged, because чай is masculine too

mistake.why: Two things at once: languages take a small letter in Russian, and the noun язык cannot be dropped. Я люблю русский язык.

sentences.usage: Saying what you study or what you are here for — the natural last line of a first introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: русский is the coat and язык is the person wearing it; Russian never sends the coat out alone.

comprehensionPool.cue: I am a student (a woman speaking)
